proof_spine: Recognize addition with seed zero and multiplication with seed one as specializations of generic reduction.
Transport reductions across pointwise-equal functions on the exact index set.
Relate finite-set reduction to membership, disjoint union, and bijective reindexing without assuming an iteration order.
Translate closed integer intervals without changing reduce order, and expose both endpoint equations.

blocks.accepted_litex:
prop reduce_assoc_comm(T set, op fn(x, y T) T):
    forall x, y, z T:
        op(op(x, y), z) = op(x, op(y, z))
    forall x, y T:
        op(x, y) = op(y, x)
forall T set, op fn(x, y T) T, seed T, A, B finite_set, f fn(x A) T, g fn(y B) A:
    $reduce_assoc_comm(T, op)
    $bijective(B, A, g)
    =>:
        finite_set_reduce(A, f, op, seed) = finite_set_reduce(B, fn(y B) T {f(g(y))}, op, seed)
blocks.reusable_lesson: The operation laws may come from any concrete prop, but their forall binders must match the law arity; reindexing consumes an already-known bijection and never invents a map.

blocks.accepted_litex:
forall T set, a, b Z, f fn(x Z) T, op fn(x, y T) T, seed T:
    a <= b
    =>:
        reduce(a, b, f, op, seed) = reduce(0, b - a, fn(k Z) T {f(a + k)}, op, seed)
        reduce(a, b, f, op, seed) = reduce(a + 1, b, f, op, op(seed, f(a)))
        reduce(a, b, f, op, seed) = op(reduce(a, b - 1, f, op, seed), f(b))
blocks.reusable_lesson: A closed_range object forgets order, but reduce uses its ascending enumeration. Equal-length translations preserve that enumeration for every operation; arbitrary bijections remain valid only through the associative-commutative finite_set_reduce route.
